title: The many revolutions of John Berger
gist: Christopher Bray reviews Tom Overton's biography John Berger: From Life on the centenary of Berger's birth, praising its archival depth but criticising its prudishness and lack of chronological structure. Bray argues Ways of Seeing was among the most influential works of late-20th-century criticism and that Berger called most major issues right before others did.

insights.claim: At the 1972 Booker prize ceremony, John Berger used his win for G. to denounce Booker McConnell's Caribbean exploitation, pledging half his £5,000 winnings to research on migrant workers and half to the British Black Panthers.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray
insights.so_what: Historic example of corporate-sponsorship reputational risk in cultural prizes.

insights.claim: Bray argues Berger's Booker outburst put what would become postcolonial studies on the intellectual map.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray
insights.so_what: Context on the intellectual origins of an influential academic field.

insights.claim: Tom Overton, who catalogued the archive Berger donated to the British Library in 2009, has had more access to Berger's life than anyone besides Berger, and uncovers new material.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray
insights.so_what: Archival access as a differentiator in biography publishing.

insights.claim: Bray criticises Overton as prudish and judgemental about Berger's serial affairs, arguing it does not follow that Berger's ideas are invalidated by failing to live up to them.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray
insights.so_what: Reflects generational shifts in moral judgement of cultural figures.

insights.claim: Bray says Overton lacks a properly chronological structure, so the biography drifts and introduces people without explanation.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray
insights.so_what: Critical reception may limit the book's appeal.

insights.claim: Bray argues Berger's 1972 Ways of Seeing did as much for feminism as Germaine Greer's The Female Eunuch and has a claim to be the most influential work of criticism of the second half of the 20th century.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray
insights.so_what: Underscores the durable cultural value of Berger's catalogue.
insights.quote: Indeed, Ways of Seeing has some claim to being the most influential work of criticism of the second half of the 20th century.

insights.claim: By introducing the concept of the male gaze, Ways of Seeing did much to invent film and media studies, and explains why arts undergraduates discuss Coronation Street as much as Coriolanus.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray
insights.so_what: Context on how a TV series reshaped humanities curricula.

insights.claim: Bray disputes Overton's claim that Berger eroded the high/low art distinction, arguing that like Adorno he believed high art hastened revolution while low art kept people in their place.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray

insights.claim: Ways of Seeing owed much to Walter Benjamin's 1935 essay on mechanical reproduction, and Berger's early criticism drew heavily on Georg Lukács.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray

insights.claim: Berger's early criticism was doctrinaire social realism, dismissing Pollock's abstracts and arguing Picasso's work thinned because wealth insulated him from ordinary people's concerns.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray
insights.so_what: Context on Berger's anti-modernist critical stance.

insights.claim: Berger abandoned his critical strictures in fiction, becoming fully experimental by G., which Bray finds unreadable and agrees shows Berger had no gift for narrative.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray
insights.so_what: His criticism, not fiction, carries the lasting value.

insights.claim: Bray says Berger moved, like Wittgenstein in reverse, from hard-headed materialist to gauzy visionary, his later work more Kantian and concerned with death not being the end.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray

insights.claim: Despite his humourlessness, Bray argues Berger called pretty much every major issue right, often before anyone else did, and remained on-point until his death aged 90 in 2017.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray
insights.so_what: Supports sustained interest in Berger's reissued works by Verso and Bloomsbury.
insights.quote: And yet: for all his over-earnestness, Berger called pretty much every major issue right.

insights.claim: Several of Berger's books are being reissued, including a uniform edition by Verso and a new Bloomsbury edition of G., to coincide with his centenary.
insights.speaker: Christopher Bray
insights.so_what: Centenary-driven backlist reissues as a publishing revenue strategy.
